claim: Several studies have estimated the human per-generation germline mutation rate using large pedigrees in the past decade.
source: In the past decade, several studies have estimated the human per-generation germline mutation rate using large pedigrees.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about the recent history of mutation rate studies.

claim: Estimates for germline mutation rates in various nonhuman species have been published recently.
source: More recently, estimates for various nonhuman species have been published.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Table 1 which lists multiple nonhuman species.

claim: Methodological differences among studies make direct comparisons of germline mutation rates difficult.
source: However, methodological differences among studies in detecting germline mutations and estimating mutation rates make direct comparisons difficult.
evidence: This is a central claim of the manuscript supported by the Mutationathon results showing variation in estimates.

claim: The Mutationathon was a competition organized among five research labs to compare germline mutation rate estimates for a single pedigree of rhesus macaques.
source: Additionally, we present the results from a 'Mutationathon,' a competition organized among five research labs to compare germline mutation rate estimates for a single pedigree of rhesus macaques.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: There was almost a twofold variation in the final estimated mutation rate among groups using different post-alignment processing, calling, and filtering criteria.
source: We report almost a twofold variation in the final estimated rate among groups using different post-alignment processing, calling, and filtering criteria, and provide details into the sources of variation across studies.
evidence: This is a key finding from the Mutationathon experiment reported in the abstract.

claim: The difference among mutation rate estimates from different groups is not statistically significant.
source: Though the difference among estimates is not statistically significant, this discrepancy emphasizes the need for standardized methods in mutation rate estimations and the difficulty in comparing rates from different studies.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the abstract as a result of statistical analysis.

claim: Germline mutations are the source of most genetic diseases.
source: Germline mutations are the source of most genetic diseases and provide the raw material for evolution.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Germline mutations provide the raw material for evolution.
source: Germline mutations are the source of most genetic diseases and provide the raw material for evolution.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: High-throughput next-generation sequencing enables direct estimation of the germline mutation rate over a single generation based on whole-genome comparison of pedigree samples.
source: The development of high-throughput next-generation sequencing offers the opportunity to directly estimate the germline mutation rate over a single generation, based on a whole-genome comparison of pedigree samples (mother, father, and offspring), without requiring assumptions about generation times or fossil calibrations (Tiley et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological capability with citation support.

claim: Pedigree-based mutation rate estimation does not require assumptions about generation times or fossil calibrations.
source: The development of high-throughput next-generation sequencing offers the opportunity to directly estimate the germline mutation rate over a single generation, based on a whole-genome comparison of pedigree samples (mother, father, and offspring), without requiring assumptions about generation times or fossil calibrations (Tiley et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the pedigree approach with citation support.

claim: Pedigree sequencing enables identification of the parental origin of mutations.
source: Furthermore, pedigree sequencing enables researchers to identify the parental origin of the mutations; that is, whether the mutation arose in the maternal or paternal germline.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of pedigree sequencing.

claim: The first estimate of the human germline mutation rate using pedigrees was published more than 10 years ago.
source: The first estimate of the human germline mutation rate using pedigrees was published more than 10 years ago (Roach et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a historical fact with citation support.

claim: The first pedigree-based mutation rate for a nonhuman primate (chimpanzee) was estimated four years after the first human estimate.
source: Four years later, the first pedigree-based mutation rate for a nonhuman primate, the chimpanzee, was estimated (Venn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a historical fact with citation support.

claim: At least 20 vertebrate species have mutation rates estimated by pedigree sequencing.
source: Today, at least 20 vertebrate species have mutation rates estimated by pedigree sequencing (Table 1), with half added in the past two years.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Table 1 which lists the species.

claim: Half of the vertebrate species with pedigree-based mutation rate estimates were added in the past two years.
source: Today, at least 20 vertebrate species have mutation rates estimated by pedigree sequencing (Table 1), with half added in the past two years.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about recent research activity.

claim: Most studies using human pedigrees have reached similar mutation rates of approximately 1.2 × 10⁻⁸ mutations per site per generation at an average age of around 30 years.
source: Although most studies using human pedigrees have now reached similar rates of ~1.2 × 10–8 mutations per site per generation at an average age of around 30 years (Table 1), the effect of different methodologies is likely to have a much larger effect on estimates in other species.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the data in Table 1.

claim: Different methodologies are likely to have a larger effect on mutation rate estimates in nonhuman species compared to humans.
source: Although most studies using human pedigrees have now reached similar rates of ~1.2 × 10–8 mutations per site per generation at an average age of around 30 years (Table 1), the effect of different methodologies is likely to have a much larger effect on estimates in other species.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the characteristics of nonhuman species studies.

claim: Nonhuman species have lower-quality genome assemblies compared to humans.
source: This is because these species have lower-quality genome assemblies, less information about segregating polymorphisms, often higher heterozygosity, and an overall deficit in prior information on mutation rates.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for methodological challenges in nonhuman species.

claim: Nonhuman species have less information about segregating polymorphisms compared to humans.
source: This is because these species have lower-quality genome assemblies, less information about segregating polymorphisms, often higher heterozygosity, and an overall deficit in prior information on mutation rates.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for methodological challenges in nonhuman species.

claim: Nonhuman species often have higher heterozygosity compared to humans.
source: This is because these species have lower-quality genome assemblies, less information about segregating polymorphisms, often higher heterozygosity, and an overall deficit in prior information on mutation rates.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for methodological challenges in nonhuman species.

claim: The key principle of the pedigree-based approach is to detect de novo mutations present in a heterozygous state in an offspring that are absent from its parents' genomes.
source: The key principle of the pedigree-based approach is to detect de novo mutations (DNMs) present in a heterozygous state in an offspring that are absent from its parents' genomes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as the fundamental principle of the method and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: A per-site per-generation mutation rate can be inferred by dividing the number of DNMs by the number of sites in the genome that mutations could possibly be identified in.
source: A per-site per-generation mutation rate can be inferred by dividing the number of DNMs by the number of sites in the genome that mutations could possibly be identified in (and accounting for the diploid length of the genome, as mutations can be transmitted by both the mother and the father).
evidence: This is stated as the calculation method for mutation rate.

claim: False-positive calls can be caused by sequencing errors, errors introduced by read mapping and genotyping steps, stochastically missing an alternative allele in a parent, or somatic mutations in the offspring.
source: False-positive (FP) calls (sites incorrectly detected as DNMs) can be caused by sequencing errors, errors introduced by read mapping and genotyping steps, stochastically missing an alternative allele in a parent, or somatic mutations in the offspring.
evidence: This is stated as sources of error in DNM detection.

claim: The overall pipeline from high-throughput next-generation sequencing data to an estimated mutation rate includes five steps: sampling and sequencing, alignment and post-alignment processing, variant calling, detecting de novo mutations, and mutation rate estimation.
source: The overall pipeline from high-throughput next-generation sequencing data to an estimated mutation rate is similar across all studies listed in Table 1. It includes five steps (Figure 2):
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The first study to estimate a pedigree-based human mutation rate used only two trios and estimated a mutation rate of 1.1 × 10⁻⁸ per site per generation.
source: The first study to estimate a pedigree-based human mutation rate used only two trios and estimated a mutation rate of 1.1 × 10–8 per site per generation (Roach et al., 2010), which is within the overall variation reported across studies with larger sample sizes (Table 1).
evidence: This is a historical fact with citation support.

claim: The mutation rate estimate from the first pedigree-based human study is within the overall variation reported across studies with larger sample sizes.
source: The first study to estimate a pedigree-based human mutation rate used only two trios and estimated a mutation rate of 1.1 × 10–8 per site per generation (Roach et al., 2010), which is within the overall variation reported across studies with larger sample sizes (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with data from Table 1.

claim: Multi-sibling pedigrees offer a unique opportunity to detect mutations that may be mosaic within one of the parents indicative of having occurred early in development.
source: Multi-sibling pedigrees (i.e., when there is more than one offspring) offer a unique opportunity to detect mutations that may be mosaic within one of the parents indicative of having occurred early in development.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of multi-sibling pedigrees.

claim: Blood is often the preferred tissue for DNA extraction because many different tissues contribute cells to the blood.
source: In this regard, blood is often the preferred tissue: as many different tissues contribute cells to the blood, the hope is that a somatic mutation in any one of them will not be mistaken for a DNM.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for tissue selection.

claim: PCR amplification can generate artifacts caused by the introduction of sequence errors or by the overamplification of some reads.
source: PCR amplification is commonly used to increase the quantity of DNA, but this can generate artifacts caused by the introduction of sequence errors (PCR errors) or by the overamplification of some reads (PCR bias) (Acinas et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a known issue with PCR with citation support.

claim: PCR-free libraries are preferable for samples yielding a sufficient amount of DNA.
source: Thus, for samples yielding a sufficient amount of DNA, PCR-free libraries that do not involve amplification prior to cluster generation are preferable.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation based on the issues with PCR.

claim: The Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (BWA) has been used in the majority of studies on direct mutation rate estimation.
source: The Burrows–Wheeler Aligner (BWA; Li and Durbin, 2009) is an algorithm developed to map short reads (50–250 bp) to a reference genome and has been used in the majority of studies on direct mutation rate estimation (Bergeron et al., 2021a; Besenbacher et al., 2019; Harland et al., 2017; Jónsson et al., 2017; Kessler et al., 2020; Koch et al., 2019; Malinsky et al., 2018; Maretty et al., 2017; Milholland et al., 2017; Pfeifer, 2017; Sasani et al., 2019; Smeds et al., 2016; Tatsumoto et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with extensive citation support.

claim: A minimum coverage of 15× has been advised to call SNPs accurately.
source: A minimum coverage of 15× has been advised to call SNPs accurately (Fumagalli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation with citation support.

claim: It is advised to aim for a minimum of 35× coverage as a rule of thumb for mutation rate studies.
source: Thus, it is advised to aim for a minimum of 35× as a rule of thumb.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation based on statistical calculations presented in the text.

claim: GATK is widely used among studies that call germline DNMs.
source: GATK (Van der Auwera and O'Connor, 2020) is widely used among studies that call germline DNMs (Bergeron et al., 2021a; Besenbacher et al., 2019; Campbell et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2017; Harland et al., 2017; Jónsson et al., 2017; Koch et al., 2019; Malinsky et al., 2018; Maretty et al., 2017; Milholland et al., 2017; Pfeifer, 2017; Sasani et al., 2019; Smeds et al., 2016; Tatsumoto et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Wong et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with extensive citation support.

claim: Most mutation rate studies restrict Mendelian violations to sites where both parents are homozygous for the reference allele and the offspring is heterozygous.
source: Most mutation rate studies restrict Mendelian violations to sites where both parents are homozygous for the reference allele (HomRef; 0/0) and the offspring is heterozygous (Het; 0/1 or 1/0) (Bergeron et al., 2021a; Besenbacher et al., 2019; Jónsson et al., 2017; Koch et al., 2019; Pfeifer, 2017; Smeds et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: One of the most straightforward methods to validate DNMs is by PCR amplification followed by resequencing such as Sanger sequencing.
source: One of the most straightforward methods to validate DNMs is by PCR amplification followed by resequencing such as Sanger sequencing to ensure the genotype of each individual of the trio (Bergeron et al., 2021a; Koch et al., 2019; Maretty et al., 2017; Tatsumoto et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a validation method with citation support.

claim: Each group of investigators in the Mutationathon detected between 18 and 32 candidate DNMs.
source: Each group of investigators implemented their own set of filters (Table 2—source data 1) and detected between 18 (CV) and 32 (SB) candidate DNMs.
evidence: This is a result from the Mutationathon experiment.

claim: After PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing validation, 33 positions were validated as true-positive DNMs, 6 were determined to be false-positive calls, and 4 did not successfully amplify.
source: After PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing validation of the DNM candidates from all research groups (43 distinct sites), we validated 33 positions as true-positive DNMs, 6 were determined to be FP calls, and 4 did not successfully amplify (Figure 3b, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiment.

claim: No group found all true-positive DNMs in the Mutationathon.
source: No group found all true-positive DNMs.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the Mutationathon.

claim: Of the 33 true-positive DNMs, only 7 were detected by all research groups.
source: Of the 33 true-positive DNMs, only 7 were detected by all research groups (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a result from the Mutationathon shown in Figure 3.

claim: The candidate DNMs found by a single group are more likely to be false positives.
source: The candidate DNMs found by a single group are more likely to be FPs as the six FP candidates revealed by the PCR experiment were all candidates detected by a single pipeline.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the validation results.

claim: The transition-to-transversion ratio did not significantly differ between groups in the Mutationathon.
source: The differences in candidate DNMs led to differences in the spectrum of mutations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), yet the transition-to-transversion ratio (ti/tv) did not significantly differ between groups (ti/tv all true-positives = 2.7; SB = 2.25; CV = 3; TT = 3.2; RW = 3.2; LB = 5.5; Fisher's exact test p-value=0.87).
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result from the Mutationathon.

claim: The transmission rate of all true-positive DNMs was 67% with 21 DNMs transmitted to the next generation, which is not significantly different from the expected 50% inheritance.
source: The transmission rate of all true-positive DNMs (33) was 67% with 21 DNMs transmitted to the next generation; this rate is not significantly different from the expected 50% inheritance (binomial test p-value=0.08).
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result from the Mutationathon.

claim: TT estimated the lowest mutation rate of 0.46 × 10⁻⁸ mutations per site per generation.
source: TT estimated the lowest rate of 0.46 × 10–8 mutations per site per generation (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a result from the Mutationathon shown in Figure 4.

claim: CV, RW, SB, and LB found similar mutation rates with 25% differences between the lowest and the highest rate and large overlap of the confidence intervals.
source: CV, RW, SB, and LB found similar rates (CV: 0.77 × 10–8; RW: 0.85 × 10–8; SB: 0.73 × 10–8; LB: 0.63 × 10–8), with 25% differences between the lowest and the highest rate and large overlap of the confidence intervals (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a result from the Mutationathon shown in Figure 4.

claim: RW estimated the highest mutation rate with 0.85 × 10⁻⁸ mutations per site per generation.
source: RW estimated the highest rate with 0.85 × 10–8 mutations per site per generation, from a relatively small set of candidates (22), yet the denominator was also small as CG represented about 50% of the autosomal genome.
evidence: This is a result from the Mutationathon.

claim: TT's pipeline was the only one to find a candidate mutation at a site where the father was heterozygous, which was validated by the PCR experiment.
source: TT's pipeline was the only one to find a candidate mutation at a site where the father was heterozygous C/G, the mother was homozygous for the reference allele G/G, and the offspring was heterozygous A/G. These genotypes were validated by the PCR experiment, indicating that a true germline mutation has arisen at a heterozygous site in a parental genome.
evidence: This is a specific result from the Mutationathon validation.

claim: The GQ filter had the largest impact on the number of mutations and the final estimated mutation rate.
source: The GQ filter had the largest impact on the number of mutations and the final estimated mutation rate.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the filter comparison analysis.

claim: The number of candidate DNMs found with GQ < 20 was three times higher than the one obtained with the most conservative GQ filter.
source: The number of candidate DNMs found with GQ < 20 was three times higher than the one obtained with the most conservative GQ filter (GQHom < 100 and GQHet < 200), and the difference was still twofold after correcting for FP calls.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the filter comparison analysis.

claim: More than 90% of the candidate DNMs were false positives with no GQ filter while no false positives were found with conservative GQ filters.
source: This filter also seems to be the most efficient at reducing the number of FP calls, estimated here with the manual curation method, as more than 90% of the candidates DNMs were FPs with no GQ filter while we found no FPs with conservative GQ filters (GQ < 80 and GQHom < 100 and GQHet < 200).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the filter comparison analysis.

claim: Two recent, independent studies of the per-generation mutation rate in rhesus macaque reported rates that were within 5% of each other for individuals of the same age.
source: On a more positive note, it is important to point out that two recent, independent studies of the per-generation mutation rate in rhesus macaque reported rates that were within 5% of each other for individuals of the same age (Bergeron et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a positive finding with citation support.

claim: The pedigree used for the Mutationathon consisted of Noot (father), M (mother), Heineken (daughter), and Hoegaarde (Heineken's daughter).
source: The macaque pedigree consisted of Noot (father), M (mother), Heineken (daughter), and Hoegaarde (Heineken's daughter) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This describes the pedigree structure used in the experiment.

claim: Each individual in the Mutationathon pedigree was sequenced with BGISEQ-500 at an average coverage between 40× and 70×.
source: Each individual was sequenced with BGISEQ-500 at an average coverage between 40× (Noot) and 70× (all other individuals).
evidence: This describes the sequencing methodology used.

claim: The list of vertebrate species with pedigree-based mutation rate estimates includes 10 primates, 5 nonprimate mammals, 1 bird, and 4 fish.
source: The list of species includes 10 primates, 5 nonprimate mammals, 1 bird, and 4 fish (see Supplementary file 1b for differences in study design and methodology).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Table 1.

source: Orangutan (Pongo abelii)	1.66	1	♂: 31.00 and ♀: 15.00	Besenbacher et al., 2019
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes)	1.201.481.26	617	♂: 18.90 and ♀: 15.00♂: 24.00 and ♀: 24.00♂: 19.30 and ♀: 15.90	Venn et al., 2014Tatsumoto et al., 2017Besenbacher et al., 2019
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Gorilla (Gorilla gorilla)	1.13	2	♂: 14.50 and ♀: 20.50	Besenbacher et al., 2019

source: Baboon (Papio anubis)	0.57	12	♂: 10.70 and ♀: 10.20	Wu et al., 2020

source: Green monkey (Chlorocebus sabaeus)	0.94	3	♂: 8.70 and ♀: 4.70	Pfeifer, 2017

source: Owl monkey (Aotus nancymaae)	0.81	14	♂: 6.60 and ♀: 6.50	Thomas et al., 2018

source: Marmoset (Callithrix jacchus)	0.43	1	~2.80	Yang et al., 2021
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Gray mouse lemur (Microcebus murinus)	1.52	2	♂: 4.55 and ♀: 1.45	Campbell et al., 2021
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Mouse (Mus musculus)	0.570.39	815	Unspecified~0.47	Milholland et al., 2017Lindsay et al., 2019
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Cattle (Bos taurus)	1.17	5	Unspecified	Harland et al., 2017
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Wolf (Canis lupus)	0.45	4	♂: 4.00 and ♀: 2.25	Koch et al., 2019
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Domestic cat (Felis catus)	0.86	11	♂: 4.70 and ♀: 2.90	Wang et al., 2021b
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus)	0.70	2	Unspecified	Martin et al., 2018
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Collared flycatcher (Ficedula albicollis)	0.46	7	Unspecified	Smeds et al., 2016
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Herring (Clupea harengus)	0.20	12	Unspecified	Feng et al., 2017
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

source: Cichlid (Astatotilapia calliptera, Aulonocara stuartgranti, and Lethrinops lethrinus)	0.35	9	Unspecified	Malinsky et al., 2018
evidence: This is data from Table 1.

claim: Approximately 3% of DNMs in humans are part of a mutation cluster.
source: In humans, ~3% of the DNMs are part of a mutation cluster (Besenbacher et al., 2016; Kaplanis et al., 2019), a feature that appears to be conserved among all eukaryotes (Schrider et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Mutation clustering appears to be conserved among all eukaryotes.
source: In humans, ~3% of the DNMs are part of a mutation cluster (Besenbacher et al., 2016; Kaplanis et al., 2019), a feature that appears to be conserved among all eukaryotes (Schrider et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The binomial probability of not observing a read with one of the alleles in a heterozygote with 15× coverage is 3.05 × 10⁻⁵.
source: For example, the binomial probability of not observing a read with one of the alleles in a heterozygote with 15× coverage is 0.515 = 3.05 × 10–5, which will happen by chance around 30× in a genome with 1 million heterozygous positions.
evidence: This is a statistical calculation presented in the text.

claim: The probability that a somatic mutation present in 10% of cells is seen in more than 30% of reads is 0.0113 with 20× coverage but falls to 0.0004 with 35× coverage.
source: Likewise, based on the binomial distribution, the probability that a somatic mutation present in 10% of cells is seen in more than 30% of reads is 0.0113 with 20× coverage but falls to 0.0004 with 35× coverage.
evidence: This is a statistical calculation presented in the text.

claim: Realignment around indels is required when calling variants with non-haplotype-aware callers but is not necessary with haplotype-aware variant callers.
source: Specifically, realignment around indels is required when calling variants with non-haplotype-aware callers (such as GATK's UnifiedGenotyper), but is not necessary with haplotype-aware variant callers (such as GATK HaplotypeCaller [Poplin et al., 2018], Platypus [Rimmer et al., 2014], or FreeBayes [Garrison and Marth, 2012]).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological guideline with citation support.

claim: BGISEQ-500 technology combines DNA nanoball nanoarrays with polymerase-based stepwise sequencing and shows similar performances to Illumina on data quality.
source: Another equivalent technology, used in two studies (Bergeron et al., 2021a; Roach et al., 2010), is BGISEQ-500, combining DNA nanoball nanoarrays with polymerase-based stepwise sequencing (Mak et al., 2017) and showing similar performances to Illumina on data quality (Chen et al., 2019; Patch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Most pedigree-based studies of germline mutations have sequenced each individual to a depth between 30× and 50×.
source: Most pedigree-based studies of germline mutations have sequenced each individual to a depth between 30× and 50× (Besenbacher et al., 2019; Campbell et al., 2021; Jónsson et al., 2017; Kessler et al., 2020; Malinsky et al., 2018; Milholland et al., 2017; Sasani et al., 2019; Smeds et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020), three studies sequenced at a higher depth of 80× (Bergeron et al., 2021a; Maretty et al., 2017) and 150× (Tatsumoto et al., 2017), while six studies sequenced at a depth lower than 25× on average (Harland et al., 2017; Koch et al., 2019; Lindsay et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2018; Pfeifer, 2017; Rahbari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with extensive citation support.

claim: Estimates of callable genome vary widely from 45% to 91.5% of the total genome across different studies.
source: However, the set of filters and input files used to infer CG differ between studies (Supplementary file 1a) and, consequently, estimates vary widely from CG representing 45% (Tatsumoto et al., 2017) to 91.5% (Malinsky et al., 2018) of the total genome.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The estimated false-negative rate ranges from 0% to 44% across different studies.
source: The methods and results differ between studies, with an estimated FNR from 0% (Smeds et al., 2016; Tatsumoto et al., 2017) to 44% (Thomas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Estimates of the false discovery rate using manual curation have varied widely depending on the study design, from 91% at low coverage to 35% at medium coverage to 11% at high coverage.
source: Estimates of the FDR using this approach have varied widely depending on the study design, from 91% (Pfeifer, 2017) at low coverage to 35% (Smeds et al., 2016) at medium coverage to 11% at high coverage (Bergeron et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The pedigree used for the Mutationathon was previously sequenced as part of a larger project on the mutation rate of rhesus macaques.
source: The pedigree used for the Mutationathon was previously sequenced as part of a larger project on the mutation rate of rhesus macaques (BioProject: PRJNA588178; Bergeron et al., 2021a).
evidence: This describes the source of the data used in the Mutationathon.

claim: Trimming was done using SOAPnuke version 1.5.6 to remove adaptors, low-quality reads, and reads smaller than 60 bases after quality control.
source: Trimming was done using SOAPnuke (RRID:SCR_015025) version 1.5.6 (Chen et al., 2018), with the following command: >SOAPnuke filter -f AAGTCGGAGGCCAAGCGGTCTTAGGAAGACAA -r AAGTCGGATCGTAGCCATGTCGTTCTGTGAGCCAAGGAGTTG –1 sequence_read_1–2 sequence_read_2 -Q 2l 10 -q 0.2 -E 60–5 0M 2 -o sequence_clean -C sequence_read_1_clean -D sequence_read_2_clean.
